variants.title: Trace the request path
variants.context: A production inference request passes through admission and routing, prefix lookup, prefill, the decode scheduler, and streaming with observation. TTFT ends when the first token reaches the client; TPOT measures later tokens; goodput measures work finished inside the SLO.
variants.prompt: A chat request arrives at a shared serving pool. Put the request path in order.

items.text: Interleave the sequence with other active sequences one decode iteration at a time.
Look up reusable KV blocks that match the model, adapter, tokenized prefix, and cache namespace.
Stream tokens to the client and record latency, cache, capacity, quality, and stop-reason evidence.
Prefill the uncached input tokens in parallel and write keys and values for every layer.
Apply tenant quotas, deadline, priority, model routing, and overload policy before any expensive work.

variants.hint: Cheap decisions and lookups come before the compute-heavy phase.
variants.explanation: Admission, prefix lookup, prefill, decode, then stream and observe; measuring each stage separately keeps a GPU win from hiding a longer queue.

variants.title: Trace the request path
variants.context: A production inference request passes through admission and routing, prefix lookup, prefill, the decode scheduler, and streaming with observation. TTFT ends when the first token reaches the client; TPOT measures later tokens; goodput measures work finished inside the SLO.
variants.prompt: A request shares a 3,000-token system prompt with thousands of others. Put the path in order and note where the shared prefix pays off.

items.text: Prefill only the tokens after the cached prefix, skipping the already computed blocks.
Report the reused tokens and the prefill milliseconds avoided, not just a cache-hit count.
Find the KV blocks for the exact 3,000-token prefix in the pool's cache namespace.
Admit the request under its tenant quota and route it to a pool serving the same model and adapter.
Decode new tokens at the normal cadence, since prefix reuse does not speed up generation.

variants.hint: Prefix reuse is concentrated in one phase.
variants.explanation: Prefix caching accelerates prefill when an exact prefix matches; decode still runs step by step, so measure tokens saved rather than hits.

variants.title: Trace the request path
variants.context: A production inference request passes through admission and routing, prefix lookup, prefill, the decode scheduler, and streaming with observation. TTFT ends when the first token reaches the client; TPOT measures later tokens; goodput measures work finished inside the SLO.
variants.prompt: A client disconnects while a long answer is streaming. Put the path in order, ending with the cancellation being honored.

items.text: The decode scheduler was interleaving the sequence with other active work.
The stream layer detects the disconnect and propagates cancellation to the worker.
The scheduler drops the abandoned sequence and releases its cache pages for queued work.
Admission bounded the request with a deadline and a cancellation owner.
Prefix lookup and prefill produced the sequence's KV state.

variants.hint: Where does the disconnect become visible, and what must be freed afterward?
variants.explanation: Cancellation must propagate to every worker so abandoned sequences release scheduler and cache capacity instead of generating tokens nobody reads.

variants.title: Admit under overload
variants.context: Continuous batching improves utilization but does not create infinite capacity. Admission is part of the optimization: classify the request at ingress, reserve memory before execution, schedule by iteration during decode, and shed overload explicitly at the boundary instead of letting timeouts decide.
variants.prompt: An interactive request arrives at a pool near its KV limit. Put the admission steps in order.

items.text: Delay, downgrade, or reject further arrivals before queues exceed the SLO.
Record tenant, priority, prompt and output bounds, streaming mode, deadline, cache eligibility, and cancellation owner.
Check model weights, runtime workspace, and the projected KV pages before admitting the sequence.
Batch it with compatible active sequences while keeping a bounded TPOT for latency-sensitive work.

variants.hint: Nothing reaches a worker before its memory is accounted for.
variants.explanation: Classify, reserve, schedule, shed: overload becomes an explicit decision made at the boundary, not a timeout discovered later.

variants.title: Admit under overload
variants.context: Continuous batching improves utilization but does not create infinite capacity. Admission is part of the optimization: classify the request at ingress, reserve memory before execution, schedule by iteration during decode, and shed overload explicitly at the boundary instead of letting timeouts decide.
variants.prompt: A 30,000-token document request arrives with batch priority while interactive traffic is active. Put the admission steps in order.

items.text: If pages run short, preempt or delay the batch request rather than letting an interactive stream time out.
Classify it as batch priority with a long prompt, a generous deadline, and no prefix eligibility.
Project its KV bytes from the prompt and output bounds and confirm the pool has the pages.
Schedule its decode iterations so interactive sequences keep their TPOT bound.

variants.hint: The batch class has its own budget and yields to the interactive class.
variants.explanation: Separate budgets for interactive and batch traffic plus a starvation bound let long work proceed without turning timeouts into the capacity policy.

variants.title: Admit under overload
variants.context: Continuous batching improves utilization but does not create infinite capacity. Admission is part of the optimization: classify the request at ingress, reserve memory before execution, schedule by iteration during decode, and shed overload explicitly at the boundary instead of letting timeouts decide.
variants.prompt: A burst of retries from an upstream gateway hits the pool. Put the admission steps in order.

items.text: Reserve memory only for the retries the pool can hold within its maximum queued tokens and predicted KV bytes.
Reject the remainder with an explicit overload response instead of queueing them past the SLO.
Classify the arrivals as internal retry traffic with its own separate budget.
Schedule the admitted retries by iteration behind deadline-ordered interactive work.

variants.hint: Retry traffic must not share the interactive budget.
variants.explanation: Overload controls specify separate budgets, a deadline-aware ordering rule, and the response returned when no route can meet the contract.

variants.title: Do the memory math
variants.context: KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes per element, where the 2 stands for keys and values. Weight memory is about parameters x bits / 8. Memory free for KV state is what remains after weights and runtime workspace.
variants.prompt: A decoder has 48 layers, 32 query heads grouped onto 4 KV heads, head dimension 128, and 2-byte cache elements. How many KV bytes does one token require across all layers?
variants.hint: Keys and values are both stored, and only KV heads count.
variants.explanation: 2 x 48 x 4 x 128 x 2 = 98,304 bytes per token before runtime layout overhead.

mistakes.feedback: Multiply by 2 for keys and values.
Use the 4 KV heads, not the 32 query heads; grouped-query attention shares KV heads.

variants.title: Do the memory math
variants.context: KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes per element, where the 2 stands for keys and values. Weight memory is about parameters x bits / 8. Memory free for KV state is what remains after weights and runtime workspace.
variants.prompt: A BF16 checkpoint occupies 32 GB of weight memory. The team quantizes it to INT4 weight-only. What is the approximate raw weight storage in GB, before scales, metadata, and padding?
variants.hint: Compare the bits per weight before and after.
variants.explanation: 16 bits to 4 bits is a fourfold reduction, so 32 GB becomes about 8 GB; scales, metadata, workspace, and KV cache still add to the footprint.

mistakes.feedback: INT4 is 4 bits, a quarter of BF16's 16 bits, not half.
Divide 16 bits by 4 bits: the ratio is 4, not 8.

variants.title: Do the memory math
variants.context: KV bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes per element, where the 2 stands for keys and values. Weight memory is about parameters x bits / 8. Memory free for KV state is what remains after weights and runtime workspace.
variants.prompt: An 80 GiB accelerator holds 16 GiB of weights and needs 4 GiB of runtime workspace. Each active sequence's projected KV state is 2 GiB. How many whole sequences can be active before overhead?
variants.hint: Reserve memory checks weights, workspace, and projected KV pages together.
variants.explanation: (80 - 16 - 4) / 2 = 30 sequences; admitting more creates preemption and a tail-latency cliff.

mistakes.feedback: Subtract the weights and workspace before dividing; the KV cache shares the device.
Runtime workspace also consumes memory; subtract it too.

variants.title: Diagnose the optimization failure
variants.context: Optimization failures hide behind healthy-looking numbers: cache entries instead of tokens saved, average benchmark scores instead of slices, raw tokens per second instead of goodput. Name the failure before tuning anything.
variants.prompt: A dashboard shows a 90% prefix-cache hit rate, yet median prefill latency has not changed since caching was enabled. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Prefill latency is dominated by the network path, not the GPU.
The cache is returning blocks for the wrong model.
The hits are tiny prefixes that avoid little prefill work.
optionFeedback: Prefill latency measures GPU processing of uncached tokens; the network is outside it.
Wrong-model blocks would be a correctness incident, not a latency one.
Counting entries instead of tokens saved makes many small hits look healthy; measure reused tokens and prefill milliseconds avoided.
variants.hint: Which unit was the dashboard counting?
variants.explanation: Measure reused tokens and prefill milliseconds avoided, not entry hits.

variants.title: Diagnose the optimization failure
variants.context: Optimization failures hide behind healthy-looking numbers: cache entries instead of tokens saved, average benchmark scores instead of slices, raw tokens per second instead of goodput. Name the failure before tuning anything.
variants.prompt: An INT4 checkpoint matches the BF16 baseline on the average benchmark, and the team wants to ship it fleet-wide. What is missing before release?
options: Nothing; the average proves quality is preserved.
Task, safety, and structured-output evaluation by slice.
A comparison at unconstrained saturation throughput.
optionFeedback: A flat average can hide a critical domain that regressed.
Quantization changes numerical representation and outputs; gate release on the slices that matter.
Throughput comparisons belong at the same SLO, and they do not test quality.
variants.explanation: Quantizing without slice evaluation is a named failure: average quality stays flat while a critical domain regresses.

variants.title: Diagnose the optimization failure
variants.context: Optimization failures hide behind healthy-looking numbers: cache entries instead of tokens saved, average benchmark scores instead of slices, raw tokens per second instead of goodput. Name the failure before tuning anything.
variants.prompt: After a scheduler change, tokens per second rose 25%, but requests completed inside the SLO stayed flat and client timeouts increased. What happened?
options: TPOT regressed because the batches are too small.
Capacity genuinely improved and the SLO needs to be relaxed.
The system is generating tokens after deadlines and cancellations.
optionFeedback: Higher tokens per second suggests larger batches, not smaller ones.
Raw tokens are not useful work; the SLO is the contract.
Optimizing raw throughput produces tokens nobody receives; track goodput and propagate cancellation.
variants.hint: Which metric counts only useful work?
variants.explanation: Goodput counts requests or tokens completed inside the SLO; raw throughput can rise while goodput stays flat.

variants.title: Choose the control for the product
variants.context: Each optimization has an operating point: the product decides which latency metric matters, cache namespaces are data-isolation boundaries, and speculative decoding only pays off where measured acceptance is high and target batches are small.
variants.prompt: A real-time voice assistant reports a healthy average of 60 tokens per second, but users complain about pauses mid-sentence. Which measurement should the team adopt?
options: Average tokens per second, sampled more often.
Tail TPOT and jitter per stream against a strict latency bound.
optionFeedback: Averages cannot describe interruptions or jitter.
Real-time voice needs strict tail latency; per-token cadence and its variance expose the pauses.
Aggregate throughput fits offline batch work, not a live voice stream.
variants.explanation: Choose the metric that matches the product: voice needs tail latency and jitter, not an average token rate.

variants.title: Choose the control for the product
variants.context: Each optimization has an operating point: the product decides which latency metric matters, cache namespaces are data-isolation boundaries, and speculative decoding only pays off where measured acceptance is high and target batches are small.
variants.prompt: Two tenants use private LoRA adapters on the same base model. The prefix cache is keyed by tokenized prefix only. What should change?
options: Nothing, because the tokenized prefix is already unique per prompt.
Disable prefix caching for all tenants to be safe.
Add model, adapter, and tenant boundary to the cache key.
optionFeedback: Two tenants can send the same words through different adapters and private state.
Caching can stay; the key needs the missing identity.
Cache namespace design is a data-isolation boundary; include adapter and tenant identity.
variants.hint: What does the key omit that changes the computed blocks?
variants.explanation: Unsafe prefix reuse comes from a cache key that omits tenant, adapter, or model identity.

variants.title: Choose the control for the product
variants.context: Each optimization has an operating point: the product decides which latency metric matters, cache namespaces are data-isolation boundaries, and speculative decoding only pays off where measured acceptance is high and target batches are small.
variants.prompt: A route already runs large efficient batches, and a trial drafter shows 35% token acceptance there. Should speculative decoding be enabled on it?
options: Yes, but only after quantizing the drafter to INT4.
Yes, everywhere, since exact speculative sampling preserves the target distribution.
No on this route; enable it only where acceptance is high and batches are small.
optionFeedback: Drafter precision does not fix low acceptance at a large-batch operating point.
Preserving the distribution says nothing about speed; drafting still costs capacity.
Drafting overhead consumes capacity when acceptance is low or the target already runs in large batches.
variants.hint: Where does the drafter's cost exceed its savings?
variants.explanation: Speculating at the wrong operating point is a named failure; enable it only on measured routes.
